we developed a new formula to estimate ionized calcium level from total calcium level in very elderly hospitalized subjects with protein malnutrition.
the new formula proposed in our article gives better results than Payne's formula, especially in the case of very elderly patients with malnutrition.

In summary, our research is concerned with
a new formula that is more appropriate for very elderly patients with low serum protein levels.
the development of a new formula to correct Ca(T) into Ca(2+) in the very elderly patients with very low albumin levels.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the formula Ca(2+) = 0.592- 0.00449 x protein (g/l) + 0.410 x total calcium (mmole/l) can be used to correct total serum calcium values into ionized serum values in very elderly in-patients.
, in the very old patients with hypoalbuminemia, Payne's formula is not appropriate and the formula proposed in this article should be used.
, for any group of hospitalized very elderly patients, the new formula for the correction of total serum calcium level into ionised serum calcium values is more accurate than Payne's formula.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the new formula is a good substitute for Payne's formula in very frail elderly patients.

, in very elderly patients, Ca(2+) is better correlated with Ca(Ad) than with Ca(T) and that, for the same total serum calcium concentration, ionized calcium level is inversely correlated with the serum protein concentration.
the best way to obtain an estimate of ionized calcium in very elderly patients is to measure total calcium and to use the formula: Ca(2+)(mmol/l)=total Ca (mmol/l)-protein (g/l)/5.
The main takeaway from our work is that
Ca(2+) should not be calculated from Ca(T) in very old patients, but rather from Ca(Ad) or from protein and albumin concentrations.
the formula we propose is more reliable than Payne's formula in very elderly patients with low albumin levels.

, for very elderly patients with low protein levels, the correction of total calcium into Ca(2+) should be performed with a formula taking into account the protein level, and not with Payne's formula.
